source.title: Bridging Critical Gaps in Convergent Learning: How Representational Alignment Evolves Across Layers, Training, and Distribution Shifts
source.authors: Chaitanya Kapoor; Sudhanshu Srivastava; Meenakshi Khosla

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests representational convergence with alignment metrics and settings different from the cited original work, including across layers, training, and distribution shifts.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own alignment results across metrics, layers, training checkpoints, and input distributions. Results cited from other work are not included as rows. Brain-data comparisons are excluded because the claim versions concern networks. The paper does not directly test whether alignment rises with model scale or capability.
record.test_reason: It measures alignment between independently seeded networks (CNNs, MoCo, ViT, Pythia) with linear, Procrustes and permutation metrics, across depth, training and OOD inputs. Its results bear on seed convergence (V3), near-linear interchangeability (V4), metric and input dependence (V6), and early, task-independent convergence and plateau (V7). It explicitly argues against the PRH task-generality explanation, which gives it some T5 character. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: the authors find orthogonal maps align nearly as well as linear ones. They find a privileged unit basis in CNNs, attributed to ReLU, but not in ViTs. They argue that early convergence, before accuracy plateaus, challenges the contravariance and task-generality (PRH) explanations, favouring shared input statistics and architectural biases.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear regression, orthogonal Procrustes, and permutation/soft-matching alignment across CNNs, ViTs, and language models, rather than reproducing either cited original study's method. It tracks layers, training checkpoints, and OOD inputs.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment scores vary with mapping restrictions (linear, Procrustes, permutation/soft-matching), and later-layer alignment changes under OOD inputs. Pearson versus Spearman correlation and center versus random spatial sampling do not materially change the reported conclusions. CNN and ViT permutation alignment also respond differently to basis rotation.
record.problems: The central comparisons are mostly between independently seeded instances of the same architecture, not models spanning different architectures, objectives, data, and modalities together. Many findings are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. Convolutional alignment uses the center pixel of each feature map rather than the full spatial representation. The OOD comparison averages across 17 datasets, and the authors note that alignment metrics may miss subtle representational changes.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows were omitted under the 60-row limit. Cited results from other work and the brain-data analysis in Appendix A8 were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep across architectures. Pythia-70m vs 160m is compared only for layer correspondence, with no trend reported.
Entire version; there is no vision–language paired data.
No stitching, relative representations, unpaired mapping or functional (downstream-loss) interchangeability.
Entire version; no interpretable features or circuits are examined.
No kNN-based measures and no neighbour-count settings.
No causal isolation of shared data or objectives; the shared-input explanation is inferred from training dynamics.

missing.what: Cross-architecture layer-by-layer Procrustes and soft-matching alignment (ResNet/VGG pairs): hierarchical correspondence holds across architectures under strict metrics
MoCo ResNet50 random rotation reduces mean permutation alignment by 14.87%
Checkpoint-to-fully-trained-reference alignment climbs sharply in epoch 1 and then levels off (ImageNet and CIFAR100)

record.verdict_notes: All comparisons are within same-architecture seed pairs, plus some cross-architecture CNN and Pythia layer maps. There is no test of scale. The Pythia result shows alignment decoupling from improving capability over training; this bears on V7 and is only indirectly relevant to V1. The basis-rotation rows are controls for basis sharing, not metric-dependence tests. The Table 1 Difference column is inconsistent with the min/max values and is probably computed per layer. Brain inter-subject analyses (A8) are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep tests whether alignment rises as models become larger and more capable; comparisons of Pythia-70m and Pythia-160m do not report that scaling trend.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language alignment test.

Tests representational alignment across seeds, including unit-order-sensitive metrics, but does not establish that the shared representations are interpretable features or establish which individual features recur.

Tests representational alignment after linear, orthogonal, and permutation/soft-matching transformations. Does not test stitching, relative representations, unpaired-data mapping, or functional interchangeability.
No test of recurrence of interpretable features, neurons, or circuits across models.
Tests dependence on alignment metric and input distribution, but not neighbour-count settings or a broad range of other similarity measures.

Tests incomplete/depth-dependent alignment, training-time plateau, and the authors' interpretation of early shared-input and architectural influences. Does not isolate shared data or objectives causally from other explanations.

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained ResNet18, ResNet50, VGG16, and VGG19 (different-seed pairs; reported collectively)
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment between same-architecture networks initialized with different seeds across network depth.
rows.value: Alignment is strongest in the earliest layers and decreases with depth; deeper layers still show significant alignment (> 0.5). The trend is stated to hold across all three metrics.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation across 5-fold cross-validation is shown in Fig. 1; numerical error values not stated.
rows.note: The text describes the trend, but the plotted layer-by-layer values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Seed pairs align strongly; deep layers still exceed 0.5. The three-metric comparison also bears on V4. Partial undersells it for V3.

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained ResNet18, ResNet50, VGG16, and VGG19 (trained versus untrained networks; reported collectively)
rows.operation_detail: Compared trained-network alignment with randomly initialized, untrained-network alignment.
rows.measure: Percentage increase in mean alignment after training
rows.value: Mean alignment increases by 145.26% in early layers and 493.84% in deeper layers.
rows.note: The text reports the percentages collectively as an example; it does not assign these percentages to individual architectures.
rows.check: Trained vs untrained is a valid baseline. Gains are +145.26% early and +493.84% deep (Procrustes, pooled models).

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, trained-versus-untrained comparison: 145.26% early and 493.84% deep

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained vision-model pairs (reported collectively)
rows.operation_detail: Compared alignment under linear regression, orthogonal Procrustes, and permutation/soft-matching constraints.
rows.measure: Alignment after optimizing the corresponding mapping
rows.value: Alignment increases in the order Permutation → Procrustes → Linear; linear mappings provide only modest improvements over Procrustes.
rows.note: The text explicitly characterizes the linear-over-Procrustes improvement as modest; plotted numerical values are not given in the text.
rows.check: For V4, Procrustes is nearly as good as linear, so the effect is observed. For V6 it is better read as partial: the ordering is by construction, and layer trends hold across metrics.

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained vision-model pairs (reported collectively)
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment using strict permutation-based matching.
rows.value: Permutation scores significantly exceed chance and are described as substantial; no numerical score is stated here.
rows.note: The text reports the above-chance result explicitly but does not provide numeric values in this passage.
rows.check: Above-chance permutation alignment is stated in text only; no number is given.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Applied a random Haar-sampled orthogonal rotation to one representation and recomputed permutation alignment.

conditions.value: minimum and maximum across convolutional layers

rows.value: Rotated: 0.154 / 0.581 (min / max); reported difference: 10.47% / 201.84% (min / max)
rows.note: The table summarizes minimum and maximum values across layers; the text says rotations almost always reduce alignment.
rows.check: This is a basis-rotation control, not a metric-choice test, so V4 and V6 links are dropped. Shared features are confirmed, but CNNs also share a basis, contrary to V3's 'not the same units/bases' qualifier. The Difference column does not equal (native−rotated)/native of the min/max values (e.g. 201.84%), so it appears to be computed per layer.

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained CNN network pairs (reported collectively)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked Procrustes alignment between networks over training epochs.
rows.value: The majority of representational convergence occurs within the first epoch, well before task performance peaks.
rows.note: The text states the qualitative trend; epoch-specific alignment values are not stated.
rows.check: Convergence is mostly complete within epoch 1, before accuracy peaks. This is the V7 'other causes' pattern in full, not partial.

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained CNN network pairs (early convolutional layers; reported collectively)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked training-related change in early-layer representational alignment.
rows.value: Early convolutional layers show little training-induced change, with alignment reducing in some cases.
rows.note: The early-layer result is stated in text; numerical changes are not given.
rows.check: Early layers are already aligned when untrained and change little with training, consistent with architecture or input explanations.

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained CNN network pairs (reported collectively)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Procrustes alignment on in-distribution and out-of-distribution images.
rows.measure: Alignment across input distributions and layer depth
rows.value: OOD inputs amplify differences in later layers; early layers maintain comparable alignment between in-distribution and OOD stimuli.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 4 reports standard error across n = 17 OOD datasets; numerical error values not stated.
rows.note: OOD effects differ by layer: later-layer alignment declines relative to early-layer stability.
rows.check: Deep-layer alignment weakens on OOD inputs while early layers hold. This is V6 input dependence. The V7 link is not apt.

rows.subject: ResNet50 models (different-seed pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Related Procrustes alignment on each OOD dataset to model task performance.
rows.measure: Correlation between alignment and OOD accuracy
rows.value: Datasets with higher maintained accuracy show stronger alignment and vice versa; the correlation is minimal in early layers and increases with network depth.
rows.note: The text states the relationship but gives no numerical correlation coefficients.
rows.check: Alignment tracks OOD accuracy in deeper layers. No coefficients are given.

rows.subject: MoCo-trained ResNet50 pair (different seeds)
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment across layers using linear, Procrustes, and permutation metrics.
rows.measure: Representational alignment by layer depth and metric
rows.value: Convergence is strongest in early layers and tapers with depth; linear and Procrustes scores remain comparable.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 6-A reports standard deviation across 5-fold cross-validation; numerical error values not stated.
rows.note: The paper describes these findings as replication of its supervised-vision pattern in self-supervised models.
rows.check: MoCo replicates the supervised pattern.

rows.subject: MoCo-trained ResNet50 pair (different seeds)

rows.value: Most alignment emerges within the first epoch, before optimal task performance.
rows.note: Qualitative finding is reported; numerical epoch values are not stated.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16 models (different-seed pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Measured [CLS]-token representation alignment across layers with linear, Procrustes, and permutation metrics.
rows.measure: Alignment by layer depth and mapping metric
rows.value: Alignment tapers with depth; Procrustes and linear scores remain comparable, and layer-wise patterns mirror those in DCNNs.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 7-A reports standard deviation across 5-fold cross-validation; numerical error values not stated.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative trends, not individual layer values.
rows.check: Procrustes is comparable to linear; alignment tapers with depth.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16 models (different-seed pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Rotated the representational basis and compared permutation alignment with the native basis.
rows.value: Native and rotated-basis permutation scores are statistically indistinguishable across layers; no common privileged basis is evident.
rows.uncertainty: Statistical indistinguishability is stated; test statistic and p-value not stated.
rows.note: This contrasts with CNN results, where random rotations reduce permutation alignment.
rows.check: The ViT shows no shared basis. This matches V3's qualifier that features are shared but bases are not. V4 and V6 links are dropped.

rows.subject: Pythia-160m models (different-seed pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Measured sentence-embedding alignment across layers with linear, Procrustes, and permutation metrics.
rows.value: Alignment follows Linear > Procrustes > Permutation; Procrustes and Linear scores are nearly identical.
rows.note: The text reports relative ordering and similarity, not numerical scores.
rows.check: For V4, Procrustes is nearly identical to linear, so observed. For V6 it is partial, since the metric ordering is expected by construction.

rows.subject: Pythia-160m models (different-seed pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-to-layer Procrustes alignment within and across language-model architectures.

conditions.value: within Pythia-160m seeds and across Pythia-70m versus Pythia-160m

rows.value: Layers at similar depths align most closely within and across architectures.
rows.note: The stated result is qualitative; no individual layer-pair scores are given.
rows.check: The within-seed part bears on V3. The 70m-vs-160m depth correspondence is cross-size but gives no scale trend.

rows.subject: Pythia models (different-seed and cross-architecture comparisons)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked Procrustes alignment across training checkpoints.
rows.value: Alignment emerges early at normalized layer indices 0, 0.5, and 1; it peaks around 8–10B tokens, then plateaus or slightly declines even as next-token prediction improves up to 300B tokens.
rows.note: The text reports the token range and trend, but not the plotted alignment values.
rows.check: Alignment peaks at 8–10B tokens, then plateaus or declines while next-token prediction keeps improving to 300B tokens. This is a full V7 plateau.
